edges.label: The flap occurred during Ruppelt's tenure and drove the record volume
edges.note: Blue Book case documentation for the 19 July 1952 Washington radar events survives; 1952 produced the largest single-year report volume of the program's history.

a.label: 1975 SAC Nuclear-Base Overflights (Loring, Wurtsmith, Malmstrom, Minot)

edges.label: Occurred six years after the Air Force closed Blue Book on a no-threat finding
edges.note: The USAF fact sheet states Blue Book was terminated on 17 December 1969 on the conclusion that no UFO had ever indicated a threat to national security. The 1975 records document unidentified objects over nuclear weapons installations.

b.label: National Air and Space Intelligence Center

edges.label: Co-located at Wright-Patterson with the successor to the Foreign Technology Division
edges.note: NASIC is the lineal successor to ATIC and FTD, the organisations that ran SIGN, GRUDGE and BLUE BOOK and exploited foreign aerospace materiel. AFRL and NASIC share the installation.

edges.label: Single Air Force science and technology laboratory, Wright-Patterson AFB
edges.note: AFRL consolidated the Wright, Phillips, Rome and Armstrong laboratories and AFOSR at Wright-Patterson - the installation named in every retrieval account since 1947.

edges.label: ATIC and every legacy UFO project were located at Wright-Patterson
edges.note: SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book were all headquartered at Wright-Patterson AFB, the site of the Air Force's foreign materiel exploitation organisation and its successors.

b.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection

edges.label: No records series has ever been identified for the JANAP channel
edges.note: Blue Book's files went to NARA; whatever accumulated on the JANAP 146 side has never been named as a series, accessioned, or searched under any disclosure statute including the FY2024 NDAA.

edges.label: Ruppelt was Blue Book's first director
edges.note: Ruppelt directed the project from March 1952 to August 1953, covering the Washington flap and the Robertson Panel, and later published the only insider account of the period.

edges.label: Hynek was scientific consultant across SIGN, GRUDGE and Blue Book
edges.note: Twenty-one continuous years as the Air Force's own astronomer on the problem — longer than any other participant in the legacy system.

edges.label: Arnold's case entered the official file series from the outset
edges.note: Army Air Forces intelligence investigated the sighting and the case documentation survives in the Blue Book record series now held at the National Archives.

edges.label: Howe is the only named witness to the AQUARIUS paper's text
edges.note: No copy of the document has ever surfaced in any archive or FOIA release; Howe's notes are the sole record of its content.

a.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection

edges.label: NARA holds the Blue Book series and is digitising legacy UFO records
edges.note: Approximately 42 cubic feet of Blue Book material on 94 rolls of microfilm (T-1206) sits alongside the new RG 615 accessions; NARA states no Blue Book document discusses Roswell.

edges.label: Recovered material routed to Air Force technical intelligence at Wright-Patterson
edges.note: Foreign Technology Division at Wright-Patterson was the designated technical exploitation centre; the Air Force felt it necessary in its January 1985 public fact sheet to deny that extraterrestrial equipment had ever been there.

edges.label: AQUARIUS and MJ-12 emerged from the same Albuquerque channel within 20 months
edges.note: The AQUARIUS paper was shown at Kirtland in April 1983; the MJ-12 film arrived postmarked Albuquerque in December 1984. Both channels ran through people in contact with AFOSI.

edges.label: GRUDGE renamed Blue Book under Ruppelt in March 1952
edges.note: Ruppelt was placed in charge of the reconstituted GRUDGE in late 1951 and the project was renamed Project Blue Book in March 1952.

edges.label: BLUE FLY provided the quick-reaction airlift for MOON DUST recoveries
edges.note: The two codewords appear together in Air Force intelligence correspondence; MOON DUST was the collection authority and BLUE FLY the transport and custody leg.

edges.label: MOON DUST was the retrieval function alongside Blue Book's public sighting file
edges.note: Blue Book was the acknowledged investigative programme; MOON DUST was a separate, quieter recovery and exploitation tasking that was never advertised to the public that Blue Book served.

edges.label: Doty showed Howe a purported classified briefing paper at Kirtland, April 1983
edges.note: Howe's contemporaneous notes record being permitted to read but not copy a document describing retrieved craft and biological entities, with a promise of film footage that was never delivered.

b.label: National Archives Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection

edges.label: Project BLUE BOOK records are held at the National Archives
edges.note: 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, T-1206, permanently transferred to NARA - the Air Force is the one agency whose UFO records were fully accessioned, and they stop in 1969.

edges.label: BLUE BOOK records transferred to the National Archives as 94 rolls of microfilm
edges.note: The records were permanently transferred to NARA and are held as 94 rolls of 35mm microfilm, T-1206.

edges.label: Air Force ran the public UFO investigation 1952-1969
edges.note: 12,618 sightings were reported to BLUE BOOK, of which 701 remain 'Unidentified'. The Secretary of the Air Force announced termination on 17 December 1969.

b.label: University of Colorado UFO Project (Condon Committee)

edges.label: Air Force funded the University of Colorado study used to close BLUE BOOK
edges.note: The termination decision rested on 'Scientific Study of Unidentified Flying Objects' and a National Academy of Sciences review of it.
